title: Find Left Most and Right Most Index of Element
description: Given a sorted array A of size N and an integer B, return [firstIndex(B), lastIndex(B)]. If B is absent return [-1, -1]. Must be O(log N).
story: Two binary searches, same shape. Once you hit the target, don't celebrate — keep walking left to find the first occurrence, then run a second BS walking right to find the last.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: scan left → right, record first and last index where A[i] == B
solutions.story: If you're allowed a single linear pass, this is the lazy answer. Two pointers — first hit goes to 'first', every hit overwrites 'last'.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
BS1 → on hit: store first, high = mid - 1
BS2 → on hit: store last,  low  = mid + 1
solutions.story: Same loop body twice, only the 'on equal' branch flips direction. Memorise: 'first hugs left, last hugs right.'

data.footer: Two-phase binary search — A = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], B = 8. First BS finds leftmost 8, second finds rightmost.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Array A = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], target B = 8. Find first and last indices where A[i] == 8. Run two binary searches: Phase 1 finds first, Phase 2 finds last.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Find First Occurrence
script.msg: Phase 1 start: low = 0, high = 5. Search the full array for the first occurrence of 8.
script.overlay: Rule: when A[mid] == B, store first = mid but keep going left: high = mid - 1.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 1
script.msg: mid = 2, A[2] = 7. Since 7 < 8, the target must be to the right → low = mid + 1 = 3.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 2
script.msg: mid = 4, A[4] = 8. Match found! Store first = 4 as a candidate, but there might be an earlier 8 → high = mid - 1 = 3.
script.overlay: On match: save the index, then search LEFT for an earlier one.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 3
script.msg: mid = 3, A[3] = 8. Another match! Update first = 3 and push high = 2. Now low > high → Phase 1 done. First occurrence = index 3.

script.label: PHASE 2 — Find Last Occurrence
script.msg: Phase 2 start: Reset search window. Now hunt for the last occurrence of 8. low = 0, high = 5.
script.overlay: Rule: when A[mid] == B, store last = mid but keep going right: low = mid + 1.

script.label: PHASE 2 — Iteration 1
script.msg: mid = 2, A[2] = 7 < 8 → go right: low = 3.

script.label: PHASE 2 — Iteration 2
script.msg: mid = 4, A[4] = 8. Match! Store last = 4 and search right for a later one → low = 5.

script.label: PHASE 2 — Iteration 3
script.msg: mid = 5, A[5] = 10 > 8 → go left: high = 4. Now low > high → Phase 2 done. Last occurrence = index 4.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = [3, 4]. First occurrence at index 3, last at 4. Two O(log N) binary searches solved the problem with no linear scan.

title: Search Insert Position (Lower Bound)
description: Sorted A, target B. If B exists return its index, else return the index of the smallest element ≥ B (or N if all are smaller).
story: This IS lower_bound dressed in interview clothes. Keep an ans = N sentinel — it auto-handles the 'insert at end' case.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: scan i = 0..N-1; first i with A[i] >= B is the answer; else N
solutions.story: Walk until something is at least as big as B. If nothing is, you append.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
ans = N
while low <= high:
  if A[mid] < B  → low = mid + 1
  else           → ans = mid, high = mid - 1
return ans
solutions.story: Whenever you find something ≥ B, lock it in as a candidate and keep looking left for an earlier one. The sentinel N is your safety net.

data.footer: Lower bound binary search — A = [1, 3, 5, 6], B = 5. Find index where 5 exists or should be inserted.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Sorted array A = [1, 3, 5, 6], target B = 5. Find the index where B exists, or where it should be inserted to maintain sorted order. This is the lower bound problem.

script.label: INITIALISE
script.msg: Set low = 0, high = 3, ans = 4 (sentinel value = N). If no element ≥ B exists, we return N meaning 'insert at end'.
script.overlay: Rule: when A[mid] ≥ B, store ans = mid and search left for an earlier position.

script.label: ITERATION 1
script.msg: mid = 1, A[1] = 3. Compare: 3 < 5 → the insert position must be to the right. Update low = mid + 1 = 2.

script.label: ITERATION 2
script.msg: mid = 2, A[2] = 5. Perfect match! 5 == 5 → return mid = 2 immediately.
script.overlay: Exact match case: when A[mid] == B, the insert position IS mid (because B already exists there).

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = 2. The target value 5 exists at index 2. If B were 4 (not present), we'd return 2 as well — the slot where 4 should be inserted.

title: Single Element in Sorted Array
description: Every element appears twice in sorted order, except one unique element. Find it in O(log N).
story: Before the unique element, pairs sit at (even, odd). After it, they shift to (odd, even). Binary search hunts for where the pattern breaks.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode:
for i in 0..N-1 step 2: if A[i] != A[i+1] return A[i]
return A[N-1]
solutions.story: Walk in twos. The first time the pair breaks, the left side is your loner.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.story: Even index + matches its neighbour = the loner is past you. Odd index + matches = the loner is behind you. Walk by 2, never by 1.

solutions.label: Alternative — XOR
solutions.pseudocode: xor all elements; pairs cancel; what's left is the loner
solutions.story: If you forget the index-parity trick, XOR every element. Duplicates annihilate, the lone one survives. Not O(log) but bulletproof.

data.footer: Index-parity binary search — A = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5]. Every element appears twice except one. Find it in O(log N).

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Array A = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5]. Every element appears twice in sorted order, except one unique element. Before the unique, pairs sit at (even, odd) indices. After it, they shift to (odd, even). Binary search finds where the pattern breaks.

script.label: CHECK BOUNDARIES
script.msg: Edge cases: A[0]=1 matches A[1]=1 ✓, A[8]=5 matches A[7]=5 ✓. Neither boundary is the loner. Search interior indices 1 to 7.
script.overlay: Pre-check: if A[0] != A[1] return A[0]. If A[N-1] != A[N-2] return A[N-1].

script.label: INITIALISE
script.msg: Set low = 1, high = 7. The search window avoids the boundary pairs.

script.label: ITERATION 1
script.msg: mid = 4 (even index), A[4] = 3, A[5] = 3. They match! Since mid is even and its pair is to the right, the pattern is still intact → unique is after this pair. Set low = mid + 2 = 6.
script.overlay: Rule: mid is even && A[mid] == A[mid+1] → unique is to the right → low = mid + 2 (skip the pair).

script.label: ITERATION 2
script.msg: mid = 6, A[6] = 4, A[5] = 3, A[7] = 5. A[6] matches neither neighbour → this is the unique element! Return 4.
script.overlay: Base case: when A[mid] != A[mid-1] AND A[mid] != A[mid+1], mid is the loner.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = 4 at index 6. The parity-check BS visited only 2 interior probes for N=9, avoiding a full linear scan.

title: Find a Peak Element
description: Find any element ≥ both neighbours. Corners count if they beat their one neighbour. Guaranteed a single peak. Solve in O(log N).
story: If you're standing on a slope, walk uphill. That direction must contain a peak. Binary search just walks uphill twice as fast.
plain: You're standing somewhere on the array. Look at the value to your left and the value to your right. Whichever side goes UP — walk that way. Keep doing this and you must reach a peak, because the array can't climb forever. Binary search lets you take giant uphill steps instead of one-by-one.
tale: A blindfolded hiker is dropped onto a strange mountain. He cannot see the summit. But at every step, his fingertips can feel whether the slope tilts up or down beside his feet. So he makes a vow: 'I will always step toward the rising ground.' The mountain is mischievous — it has hidden valleys and false flats — but it has exactly one peak. As long as the hiker keeps choosing the rising side, the mountain itself is funnelling him to the summit. He doesn't need to see. He just needs to trust the slope.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.plain: Walk the array from left to right. At every index, check whether both neighbours are smaller. The first such element is a peak. Handle the two corners separately (they have only one neighbour).
solutions.tale: A patient watchman walks the whole ridge from sunrise. He stops at every rock and looks both ways. The moment he finds a rock taller than its two neighbours, he plants his flag and goes home.
approach: If N == 1, the only element is the peak.
Check the left corner: if A[0] >= A[1], return A[0].
Check the right corner: if A[N-1] >= A[N-2], return A[N-1].
Loop i from 1 to N-2 and return the first A[i] that is >= both A[i-1] and A[i+1].
solutions.pseudocode: scan; return A[i] when both neighbours are smaller
solutions.story: Just look. Linear and obvious.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use binary search. At the midpoint, compare with both neighbours. If mid beats both, you found a peak. Otherwise look at the slope: if A[mid] > A[mid-1] you're climbing, so a peak must lie to the right — throw away the left half. Otherwise throw away the right half. Repeat until you land on the peak.
solutions.tale: The blindfolded hiker grows impatient. Instead of one step at a time, he teleports to the middle of the unexplored stretch and feels the slope. If it rises, he abandons everything behind him — the peak cannot be in flat or downhill territory. If it falls, he abandons everything ahead. Half the mountain disappears with each teleport. In a handful of jumps, he is standing on the summit.
approach: Handle N == 1 and both corner cases up front so the loop never touches an out-of-bound neighbour.
Set low = 1, high = N - 2 (the safe interior range).
While low <= high, compute mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
If A[mid] is greater than both A[mid-1] and A[mid+1], return A[mid] — you are on the peak.
Else if A[mid] > A[mid-1], the slope rises to the right, so push low = mid + 1.
Otherwise the slope falls, so a peak must be on the left: high = mid - 1.
solutions.pseudocode:
Pre-check both boundaries.
Loop low=1, high=N-2:
  if A[mid] beats both neighbours → return A[mid]
  else if A[mid] > A[mid-1]      → climbing, go right
  else                            → descending, go left
solutions.story: Don't think 'find target'. Think 'walk toward higher ground'. A peak must exist in the direction of increase.

data.footer: Hand-authored walkthrough — A = [5, 17, 100, 11]. Algorithm: O(log N) peak BS.

script.label: Setup
script.msg: Array A = [5, 17, 100, 11]. A peak is any element ≥ both its neighbours. Corners count if they beat their one neighbour. We'll first rule out the two corners, then binary-search the interior.

script.label: Corner check ⓛ — left edge
script.msg: Look at the left corner: A[0]=5 vs A[1]=17. Is 5 ≥ 17? No — the slope rises away from index 0, so it cannot be a peak.
script.overlay: Rule: A[0] >= A[1] ? If yes → return A[0]. Here 5 < 17, so skip.

script.label: Corner check ② — right edge
script.msg: Look at the right corner: A[3]=11 vs A[2]=100. Is 11 ≥ 100? No — the slope rises away from index 3 too.
script.overlay: Rule: A[N-1] >= A[N-2] ? Here 11 < 100, so skip. Both corners ruled out → enter interior BS.

script.label: Initialise interior search
script.msg: Interior range: low = 1, high = N-2 = 2. Search window is just indices 1 and 2. Both corners are now permanently eliminated.
script.overlay: Why low=1, high=N-2? So mid-1 and mid+1 are always safe — no out-of-bounds neighbour.

script.label: Iteration 1 — pick mid
script.msg: mid = 1 + (2-1)/2 = 1. Inspect A[1] = 17 and its neighbours A[0]=5, A[2]=100.

script.label: Iteration 1 — compare neighbours
script.msg: Is A[1]=17 greater than both neighbours? A[0]=5 ✓ but A[2]=100 ✗. Not a peak. Check the slope direction: A[1]=17 vs A[mid-1]=A[0]=5. 17 > 5 → we are climbing rightward.
script.overlay: Decision: slope climbs right → a peak must lie to the right → set low = mid + 1 = 2.

script.label: Iteration 2 — window shrinks
script.msg: low = 2, high = 2. Only one cell left in the interior. mid = 2. Inspect A[2] = 100.

script.label: Iteration 2 — peak found
script.msg: A[2]=100 vs A[1]=17 and A[3]=11. 100 > 17 ✓ and 100 > 11 ✓ — beats both neighbours. Return 100.
script.overlay: Trace summary: corners skipped → 1 BS iteration narrowed to index 2 → peak. Visited 2 interior probes for N=4, vs 4 for brute scan.

script.label: Done
script.msg: ✅ Answer = 100 at index 2. The hiker took giant uphill jumps — at every probe he asked only one question: which side rises? — and the mountain funnelled him to the summit in O(log N).

title: Matrix Search
description: N×M matrix, rows sorted left-to-right, each row's first element ≥ previous row's last. Return 1 if B exists, else 0.
story: Pretend the matrix is one long sorted array of length N*M. Binary search on that virtual array. Convert index → (row, col) on the fly: row = idx / M, col = idx % M.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
low = 0, high = N*M - 1
while low <= high:
  mid = ...; r = mid/M; c = mid%M
  compare A[r][c] with B and shrink as usual
solutions.story: Flat indexing turns 2D into 1D for free. The whole sorted property of the matrix is just one BS away.

title: Minimum Difference
description: Matrix C of A×B. For each adjacent row pair, find the minimum absolute difference between any element of row i and any element of row i+1. Return the smallest such diff.
story: Sort each row, then for every element pick its closest neighbour in the next row using lower_bound. Track the smallest |diff| globally.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
sort each row
for each i, j:
  lb = lower_bound(C[i+1], C[i][j])
  consider |C[i][j] - C[i+1][lb]|     (closest greater)
  consider |C[i][j] - C[i+1][lb-1]|   (closest smaller)
  update ans = min
solutions.story: Closest = one of two: the first element ≥ you, or the one right before it. Lower bound gives you both for free.

title: Maximum Height of Staircase
description: Given A blocks, build max-height staircase where stair i needs i blocks. Find max h such that 1+2+...+h ≤ A.
story: h·(h+1)/2 ≤ A. Either solve the quadratic, binary search on h, or just walk one stair at a time. All three work.

solutions.label: Brute (greedy walk)
solutions.pseudocode:
x = 1, steps = 0
while A >= x: A -= x; steps++; x++
return steps
solutions.story: Just keep buying the next stair until you can't afford it. Surprisingly fast — only ~√(2A) stairs exist.

solutions.label: Optimal (BS on answer)
solutions.pseudocode: low=0, high=sqrt(2A)+1; find max h with h*(h+1)/2 <= A
solutions.story: Classic BS on answer. Predicate is monotonic — once h is too tall, every larger h is also too tall.

data.footer: BS on answer — find max h with h×(h+1)/2 ≤ 20. Answer = 5 (staircase uses 1+2+3+4+5=15 blocks).

title: Square Root of Integer
description: Compute floor(sqrt(A)) without using Math.sqrt. A up to 1e9 means mid*mid overflows int — use long.
story: Largest x with x·x ≤ A. Standard BS on answer. The only trap is integer overflow when squaring mid.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: for x = 0..: if x*x > A return x - 1
solutions.story: Linear scan until you overshoot.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode: low=1, high=A/2; track largest mid with mid*mid <= A (as long)
solutions.story: Use long for the multiplication. A/2 is a sharper upper bound than A.

title: Rotated Sorted Array Search
description: Sorted array rotated at unknown pivot. Find target index in O(log N). No duplicates.
story: First find the rotation pivot with BS (smallest element). Then you know which sorted half contains B and run a normal BS on that half.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: linear scan
solutions.story: If it's small, scan it. Otherwise it's a sin.

solutions.label: Optimal — pivot + BS
solutions.pseudocode:
k = rotationFactor(A)   // index of smallest element
if B == A[0] return 0
if B > A[0] → search [0, k-1]
else        → search [k, N-1]
solutions.story: Pivot splits the array into two sorted halves. A[0] tells you which half B lives in. Then it's vanilla BS.

data.footer: Rotated sorted array search — A = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], B = 0. Find pivot (min element), then BS in the correct half.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Array A = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target B = 0. Originally sorted, then rotated at unknown pivot. Strategy: (1) Find pivot (index of min element). (2) Decide which half contains B. (3) Run normal BS on that half.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Find Pivot
script.msg: Phase 1: Find rotation pivot (smallest element). Compare A[mid] with A[0]: if A[mid] ≥ A[0], the left half is sorted → pivot is to the right.
script.overlay: Pivot rule: A[mid] >= A[0] → pivot in right half → low = mid + 1. Else pivot in left half or IS mid.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 1

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description: Two sorted arrays A, B. Return the median of the merged sequence. Must run in O(log(min(M,N))).
story: Don't merge. Binary search a partition on the smaller array such that everything on the left of both arrays ≤ everything on the right. The median falls out of the four boundary values.

solutions.label: Brute — merge and pick
solutions.pseudocode: merge using two pointers; return middle (or avg of middle two)
solutions.story: Easy and correct but doesn't meet the log requirement.

solutions.label: Optimal — BS on partition
solutions.pseudocode:
Ensure A is the smaller array.
low=0, high=|A|; leftCount = (M+N+1)/2
Loop:
  pX = (low+high)/2; pY = leftCount - pX
  4 boundary values (use ±∞ at edges)
  if maxLeftX <= minRightY && maxLeftY <= minRightX: done
  else if maxLeftX > minRightY: high = pX - 1
  else: low = pX + 1
solutions.story: Slice both arrays into 'left' and 'right' halves. Valid slice = each side's max ≤ the other side's min. Median pops out of the four corner values.

data.footer: Partition-based binary search — two sorted arrays, find median in O(log(min(M,N))).

title: Matrix Median
description: N×M matrix, each row sorted (rows independent). N*M is odd. Find the overall median without extra memory.
story: Don't sort the matrix. Guess a value v, count how many elements ≤ v across all rows (each row uses BS). The smallest v with count > N*M/2 is the median.

solutions.label: Brute — flatten and sort
solutions.pseudocode: copy to flat array; sort; return middle
solutions.story: Works but violates 'no extra memory'.

solutions.label: Optimal — BS on value range
solutions.pseudocode:
low=1, high=1e9; need = N*M/2
Loop:
  mid = ...
  count = sum over rows of lowerBound(row, mid)
  if count > need: high = mid - 1
  else: ans = mid; low = mid + 1
return ans
solutions.story: Binary search the VALUE, not the position. For each guess, count things ≤ it. The median is the smallest value with enough things below it.

title: ADD OR NOT
description: Array A of N ints, budget B. Each op: +1 to any element. Maximize the count of some target value (preferring smaller value on ties). Return [count, value].
story: Sort first. For each value A[i] as the target, BS the largest window ending at i that can be raised to A[i] using ≤ B ops. Use a prefix sum to compute the cost in O(1).

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
sort; prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + A[i]
for each i:
  BS cnt in [1..i+1]:
    cost = A[i] * cnt - (prefix[i+1] - prefix[i - cnt + 1])
    if cost <= B → feasible, try larger cnt
  update [count, value]
solutions.story: Cost to raise the last `cnt` numbers to A[i] = A[i]*cnt − their sum. Prefix sum makes that O(1). BS the largest feasible cnt.

title: Ath Magical Number
description: Numbers divisible by B or C are 'magical'. Return the Ath smallest magical number modulo 1e9+7.
story: Binary search the value. Count of magical numbers ≤ x = x/B + x/C − x/LCM(B,C). Smallest x with count ≥ A is the answer.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
lcm = B*C / gcd(B,C)
low=2, high=A*min(B,C)
mid = …; count = mid/B + mid/C - mid/lcm
if count >= A: ans = mid; high = mid - 1
else:           low = mid + 1
return ans % MOD
solutions.story: Inclusion-exclusion gives 'how many magicals ≤ x' in O(1). BS shrinks to the smallest value with enough.

title: Painter's Partition
description: N boards, A painters, B time per unit. Each painter paints contiguous boards. Minimize total time. Return ans % 10000003.
story: Binary search the max work any single painter does. Greedily check: walk left→right, start a new painter whenever the current load would exceed mid. If painters used ≤ A, mid is feasible.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
low = max(C), high = sum(C)
mid = candidate time
if canPaint(mid): ans = mid; high = mid - 1
else:              low = mid + 1
return (ans * B) % MOD

canPaint(time):
  painters = 1, run = 0
  for board in C:
    if run + board > time: painters++; run = board
    else                   run += board
    if painters > A: return false
  return true

title: Aggressive Cows
description: Place B cows in N stalls (positions in A). Maximize the minimum distance between any two placed cows.
story: Binary search the minimum distance. For each guess d, greedily place cows: first at A[0], each next at first stall ≥ lastPlaced + d. If B cows fit, try larger d.
plain: You have a row of stalls along a line and a herd of angry cows. You want every pair of cows to be as far apart as possible — specifically, you want the SMALLEST gap to be as big as you can make it. Guess a gap d. Walk the stalls left to right placing a cow each time you've travelled at least d from the last cow. If you can fit all B cows, the gap is achievable — try a bigger one. If not, shrink it. Binary search finds the largest d that still works.
tale: In a long stable, a farmer keeps B cows who despise each other. Put any two close and they kick the wood until it splinters. The farmer has stalls at uneven positions and one question: how far apart can I FORCE them to be, in the worst pair? He plays a game with himself. 'Could I keep them 13 paces apart?' He walks the stalls, dropping a cow only when 13 paces have passed since the last. If all B cows find a home, he smiles — maybe 14 would work too. If they don't fit, he tries 12. The farmer is doing binary search on the cows' patience.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Sort the stall positions. The answer lies somewhere between 1 and (last - first). Binary search this range. For each midpoint d, run a greedy check: place the first cow at stalls[0], then each next cow at the first stall whose position is at least d away from the last placed cow. Count how many cows you placed. If that count >= B, d is feasible — record it and push low up. Otherwise pull high down.
solutions.tale: The farmer sorts the stalls by position so his walk is one straight march. He picks a candidate distance, tries it once with a greedy hand — first cow at stall one, then skip ahead until the wood is far enough away, then drop the next — and counts. If all his cows found peace, he raises his ambition. If not, he lowers it. Each round halves the uncertainty until only one answer remains.
approach: Sort the stall array A so positions are monotonic.
Set low = 1, high = A[N-1] - A[0] — the search space for the minimum distance.
While low <= high, take mid = (low + high) / 2 as the candidate gap d.
Run canPlace(d): start with one cow placed at A[0] and lastPlaced = A[0]. Walk i = 1..N-1; whenever A[i] - lastPlaced >= d, place a cow there and update lastPlaced.
If the placed count reaches B, the gap d works — store result = mid and push low = mid + 1 to chase a bigger gap.
Otherwise the gap is too greedy — pull high = mid - 1 and try again.
When low > high, result holds the maximum minimum distance.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort A
low = 1, high = A[N-1] - A[0]
mid = candidate distance
if canPlace(mid): ans = mid; low = mid + 1
else:              high = mid - 1
solutions.story: Opposite direction from painter's: maximize on success → go right. Predicate is greedy fit-them-in.

title: Allocate Books
description: N books with page counts, B students. Allocate contiguous books minimizing the max pages any student reads. Return -1 if impossible.
story: Same skeleton as painter's. low = largest single book (a student must read at least that), high = sum. Minimize on success.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
edge: students > books → -1
low = max(book), high = sum(books)
if canAllot(mid): ans = mid; high = mid - 1
else:              low = mid + 1

canAllot(max):
  students = 1, run = 0
  for pages in books:
    run += pages
    if run > max: students++; run = pages
    if students > B: return false
  return true
solutions.story: Twin of painter's partition. If you can solve one you solve both.

title: Special Integer
description: Find max K such that NO subarray of size K has sum > B.
story: Binary search K. Predicate uses a sliding window of length K — if any window's sum exceeds B, K is too big.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
low = 0, high = N
mid = candidate K
if allWindowsOk(mid): K = mid; low = mid + 1
else:                  high = mid - 1

allWindowsOk(K):
  if K == 0 return true
  build first window sum
  slide; if any sum > B return false
  return true
solutions.story: Predicate is monotonic: if length K is bad, all longer lengths are also bad (they contain a bad K-window).
